subject: Biology
title: Life History Strategies: r-Selected vs K-Selected Species
topic: Opportunistic Proliferators vs Equilibrium Competitors, Survivorship Curves (Type I, II, III), & Trade-Offs
quickSummary: Life history strategies: Organisms evolve reproductive adaptations to maximize Darwinian fitness (r). r-Selected species (opportunistic proliferators): Unstable habitats, small body size, short lifespan, produce many small offspring, minimal parental care, Type III survivorship (insects, weeds, oysters). K-Selected species (equilibrium competitors): Stable crowded habitats near K, large body size, long lifespan, produce few large offspring, extensive parental care, Type I survivorship (elephants, primates, humans, trees).

summaryBox.title: Quick Section Summary
summaryBox.takeaway: Organisms evolve distinct life history traits: r-selected species maximize reproductive rate (r) with many small offspring and low care in disturbed habitats; K-selected species maximize competitive ability near carrying capacity (K) with few large offspring and high parental investment.

conceptBreakdown.codeSnippet:
LIFE HISTORY STRATEGIES
                                      │
         ┌────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────┐
         ▼                                                         ▼
   r-SELECTED SPECIES                                        K-SELECTED SPECIES
   (Opportunistic Proliferators)                             (Equilibrium Competitors)
   ├── Unstable, unpredictable habitats                      ├── Stable, predictable habitats
   ├── High r, small body size                               ├── Low r, large body size
   ├── Produces many small offspring                         ├── Produces few large offspring
   └── Low/No parental care (Insects, Oysters)               └── High parental care (Elephants, Humans)
conceptBreakdown.content:
### 4.1 Evolutionary Trade-Offs in Reproduction
- Natural selection operates on life histories to maximize reproductive output and **Darwinian Fitness (high $r$ value)** within environmental constraints.
- Energetic limitations create trade-offs between **offspring number vs. offspring size / parental investment**.

### 4.2 Comparative Matrix: $r$-Selection vs. $K$-Selection

| Trait / Feature | $r$-Selected Species (Opportunistic) | $K$-Selected Species (Equilibrium) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Habitat Type** | Unstable, temporary, unpredictable, disturbed | Stable, permanent, predictable, crowded |
| **Population Size ($N$)** | Fluctuates wildly (boom-and-bust); often below $K$ | Sustained near carrying capacity ($N \approx K$) |
| **Body Size & Lifespan** | Small body size; short, rapid life cycles | Large body size; long, multi-year lifespans |
| **Reproductive Age** | Early sexual maturity (precocious reproduction) | Delayed sexual maturity; late reproduction |
| **Offspring Strategy** | Produces **many small offspring** in a single event | Produces **few large offspring** over multiple seasons |
| **Parental Care** | Absent or minimal | Extensive, high energetic parental investment |
| **Survivorship Pattern** | **Type III Curve** (heavy early juvenile mortality) | **Type I Curve** (low juvenile mortality; die in old age) |
| **Representative Taxa** | Insects, annual weeds, marine pelagic fish, oysters | Elephants, primates, whales, humans, climax forest trees |

### 4.3 Ecological Survivorship Curves
- **Type I (Convex Curve)**: High survivorship throughout early and middle life; mortality increases sharply in old age (*Humans, large mammals*).
- **Type II (Diagonal / Linear Curve)**: Constant, uniform mortality rate throughout all life stages (*Songbirds, hydra, lizards*).
- **Type III (Concave Curve)**: Extremely high mortality among juveniles/larvae; the few individuals surviving past youth exhibit high adult longevity (*Oysters, frogs, marine fish, trees*).

conceptBreakdown.heading: Semelparity vs Iteroparity
conceptBreakdown.title: Semelparity vs Iteroparity
conceptBreakdown.content: Semelparous species reproduce once in their lifetime and then die (Big Bang reproduction: Pacific Salmon, Bamboo, Agave); Iteroparous species reproduce repeatedly across multiple successive breeding seasons (Birds, Mammals, Perennial trees).

conceptBreakdown.heading: Grime's CSR Plant Life History Triangle
conceptBreakdown.title: Grime's CSR Plant Life History Triangle
conceptBreakdown.content: J.P. Grime classified plant strategies into: (1) Competitors (low stress, low disturbance, dense canopies); (2) Stress-tolerators (high stress, low disturbance, e.g., lichens, alpine plants); (3) Ruderals (low stress, high disturbance, rapid weedy colonizers).
